title: Would you use Kafka or a traditional queue (SQS/RabbitMQ) for this?
summary: Tests whether the choice is grounded in replay needs and consumer count — Kafka's retained-log model — versus simple task distribution, a queue's delete-on-ack model.

slides.markdown:
"Kafka is just a better queue" is the misconception this question is checking for. It isn't a faster or fancier SQS — it's a different model entirely: a **retained, replayable log** with independent consumer groups, versus a queue's **delete-on-ack** model built for simple work distribution.

The right answer names which model the use case actually needs, not which one sounds more sophisticated.

Ask: **do multiple independent consumers need the same events**, and **do you need replay or an audit trail**? Or is this **one producer, one job, done once and discarded**?

The first pattern is Kafka's strength; the second is exactly what a plain queue is built for, more simply and with less operational overhead.

**Kafka** for multi-consumer, replayable event logs — many independent readers, each tracking its own position, able to go back and reread history. **A queue** (SQS/RabbitMQ) for simple work distribution — one logical consumer pool, each message consumed once and deleted.

The deciding factor is almost never throughput; it's whether you need multiple independent readers and replay.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: two events, two right answers
slides.markdown:
| Scenario | Consumers | Right choice |
|---|---|---|
| `order_placed` event needed by billing, shipping, and analytics | 3 independent readers, each replays if needed | Kafka — each consumer group reads independently |
| Image-resize task queue, one producer, one worker pool | 1 logical consumer, each task done once | SQS — delete-on-ack, no replay needed |

Same category of problem ("something needs to react to an event"), opposite right answers, because the consumer shape is different.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: a concrete replay scenario
slides.markdown:
Analytics needs to reprocess 30 days of `order_placed` events after a bug in their aggregation logic. Because Kafka retains the log, they replay from an earlier offset without asking the producer to resend anything — the data is just sitting there.

An SQS-based pipeline would have nothing left to replay: messages are deleted on ack, so once billing and shipping consumed them, they're gone. Analytics would need a separate archival mechanism it doesn't have.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: the operational cost difference
slides.markdown:
Kafka needs partition and consumer-group management, and a cluster to run — self-hosted or via Amazon MSK, but management overhead either way. SQS is a fully managed, near-zero-ops primitive for a single work queue: no partitions to size, no consumer-group rebalancing to reason about.

This is real cost, not incidental — picking Kafka for a use case that doesn't need its model means paying that overhead for nothing.

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud
slides.markdown:
Kafka's replayability and fan-out come at the cost of operational complexity and a steeper mental model — offsets, consumer groups, partitions — that a plain queue never asks of you. Choosing Kafka means the team signs up for that complexity permanently, not just at launch.

That's a fair price when multiple independent consumers and replay are real requirements; it's dead weight when they aren't.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: a new audit-trail requirement shows up — does that change the choice?
slides.markdown:
Yes, and worth reconsidering seriously — an audit trail is exactly Kafka's strength (replay + retained history), so a requirement like this is a strong signal to revisit an SQS-based design rather than bolt replay onto it after the fact.

The honest move in an interview is to say so directly: "if that requirement is real and permanent, I'd lean toward Kafka now rather than retrofit it later."

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: could you get Kafka-like replay out of SQS without switching?
slides.markdown:
Only partially — for example, archiving processed messages to S3 as they're consumed, then building your own replay tooling that reads from that archive. It works, but you're hand-rolling exactly what Kafka's log gives you natively.

That's a legitimate stopgap for a one-off need; as a permanent pattern, it's a sign the underlying requirement was Kafka's use case all along.

**Wrong belief:** "Kafka is the modern standard, so it's the safer choice even for a single consumer with no replay need."

**Why it's wrong:** you've bought cluster-operations overhead — partition sizing, consumer-group management, a cluster to run — for a use case that needed none of Kafka's actual strengths.

**Correct model:** default to the simpler primitive (a queue) and upgrade to Kafka only when a concrete requirement — multiple independent consumers, replay, audit trail — actually needs it.

Kafka for multi-consumer, replayable event logs; a queue for simple, single-consumer work distribution. Name the deciding factor — independent readers and replay, not throughput — and the operational cost Kafka asks for in exchange.

For how a queue and a pub/sub topic differ once you've decided you need fan-out, see [queues vs pub/sub](queues-vs-pubsub).
